The Confederate Army was the military force of the Confederate States of America during the American Civil War from 1861 to 1865. It consisted primarily of volunteers and conscripts from Southern states. Formally established in March 1861 as the military arm of the Confederacy, it initially comprised state militias and volunteer units before transitioning to a conscript army as the war dragged on. The army was organized around regional forces: the Army of Northern Virginia, most celebrated and led by Robert E. Lee; the Army of Tennessee; the Army of the Mississippi; and smaller regional commands. This decentralized structure reflected the Confederacy's weak federal authority. Many officers had served in the Mexican-American War or as career U.S. Army officers, bringing institutional knowledge and battlefield proficiency. Leaders like Robert E. Lee demonstrated remarkable tactical prowess. The Confederacy achieved significant early victories, most notably at the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861, which shattered Northern expectations of a quick victory and demonstrated Southern military competence. The Confederate forces relied heavily on interior lines of communication and the defensive advantage of fighting on home territory. They conducted brilliant tactical maneuvers and held positions despite being outnumbered, particularly in Virginia and Tennessee. However, the army suffered from chronic supply shortages, lacked industrial capacity to replace losses, and experienced declining morale as the war progressed and Union armies penetrated deeper into the South. In 1862, the Confederacy introduced conscription—the first U.S. military draft—which caused resentment among conscripts and highlighted desperation as volunteer recruitment dried up. The army surrendered in phases between April and May 1865 as Union armies pressed from multiple directions. Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House in April 1865, effectively ending organized Confederate resistance.
